questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presented with a 1-week of fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He was not dyspneic but had noticed night sweats, weight loss, and a nonproductive cough without hemoptysis. He had been diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphocytic leukemia 2 months previously and had had a prolonged neutropenia. He was taking levofloxacin, fluconazole, valaciclovir, and trimethoprim– sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis. On examination, his temperature was 102°F (38.8°C), his blood pressure was 120/60 mmHg, heart rate was 110 beats/ minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths/minute with oxygen saturations 95% on room air. He was pale but in no acute distress except for discomfort from right-sided chest pain. His lung sounds were clear bilaterally without wheezes, rales, or crackles. There was no pedal edema, but there were some scattered petechiae on his lower extremities. Investigations: Total white cell count 0.1 ×109/L Absolute neutrophil count 0.2 ×109 /L Hemoglobin 6 g/dL Platelets 67 ×109 /L Urea, creatinine, and electrolytes were within normal limits Blood cultures: no growth at 48 hours CT chest revealed numerous nodules clustered in the right lower lobe, with surrounding halos.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary aspergillosis Pulmonary aspergillosis is one of the most common invasive fungal infections in patients with hematologic malignancies, especially in those with prolonged neutropenia. Fluconazole unfortunately does not provide adequate prophylaxis. Voriconazole or posaconazole are recommended prophylaxis. The pulmonary nodules with surrounding halos are consistent and should raise suspicion for this infection. PCP is incorrect, because trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis is extremely effective for the prevention of Pneumocystis, he is not hypoxemic, and usual CT imaging findings with PCP consist of bilateral interstitial infiltrates rather than nodules with halo sign. Streptococcal pneumonia would be unusual in patients on levofloxacin prophylaxis, blood cultures are negative, and the imaging findings are not consistent with streptococcal pneumonia. Cytomegalovirus pneumonitis is rare and would be a consideration, but CT findings are not consistent. Interstitial infiltrates are usually seen rather than nodules with halos. Septic pulmonary emboli may manifest as nodules on CT chest, especially at the periphery, but the surrounding halos are not consistent, and blood cultures are negative for common bacterial pathogens.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q42

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man developed neutropenic fevers, right toe redness, and multiple skin lesions. He had received an allogenic stem cell transplant 2 months earlier with no neutropenic recovery for relapsed acute myelogenous leukemia despite multiple chemotherapy regimens. He lived in Chicago, Illinois. On examination, his temperature was 39.8°C. His right toe was erythematous and tender, and he had multiple tender nodular skin lesions with erythematous base scattered over his trunk and extremities. Investigations: MRI right toe: bone erosions Skin biopsy culture grew fungal colonies that on lactophenol blue stain appeared as in the following image: Biopsy specimen on GMS stain showed septate and branching filamentous hyphae with evidence of angioinvasion. Fungal blood cultures also grew mold.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: Fusarium spp. Fevers with disseminated skin lesions in neutropenic patients, especially hematologic malignancy, raise concern for disseminated infection (bacterial and fungal). Considering poor prognosis, prompt diagnosis and administration of antifungals is critical. Biopsy and stain showing septate hyphae with canoeshaped macroconidia are consistent with Fusarium infection. These infections often start as onychomycosis in the toes. Treatment will include empirical amphotericin B and voriconazole until further speciation is performed. Epidemiology is concerning for Blastomyces, but the stain rules out other fungal etiologies, and the skin biopsy would show yeast not hyphae. Aspergillus should be considered in neutropenic patient with fevers. However multiple skin lesions, toe infection, and stain are not consistent with it. Mucormycosis is associated with invasive sinusitis in an immunocompromised host, but dissemination to skin is not common, and the biopsy is more consistent with hyaline hyphomycete than a zygomycete. Presence of mold rules out Cryptococcus. (Image from Narayanan G, Nath R. Mayo Clinic Proc . 2016;91(4):542–543. © 2016.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q2

needs: Chapter 312 — Infections in HCT and Cellular Therapy Recipients
questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with chronic myelogenous leukemia received an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Her course was complicated by multiple episodes of graft-versus-host disease. She received courses of methylprednisolone. She was on maintenance immunosuppression with cyclosporine. On day 132, she developed fever and patchy pulmonary infiltrates and rapidly progressed into respiratory failure. She was intubated and underwent bronchoscopy. Branched hyphae were noted on the wet mount from the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid. The patient was commenced on liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg daily). Four days later the laboratory reported that the BAL culture grew Scedosporium apiospermum. The patient continued having fevers, and her respiratory status was not improving.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Increase the dose of amphotericin B to 10 mg/kg daily

questions.explanation: Switch to voriconazole Scedosporium apiospermum is resistant to amphotericin B and the echinocandins. Voriconazole is the treatment of choice. Posaconazole may be used as an alternative agent. In contrast to Scedosporium apiospermum, Scedosporium prolificans (now called Lomentospora prolificans) is resistant to all antifungals. Combination treatment with amphotericin B and echinocandins or terbinafine may be of benefit due to the potential synergistic activity in L. prolificans infection.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q30

needs: Chapter 313 — Infections in Solid Organ Transplant Recipients
questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman presented with dyspnea associated with nonproductive cough. She rapidly progressed to acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. She had received an orthotopic liver transplant 3 months previously for cirrhosis due to autoimmune hepatitis. The donor was a 28-year-old man who died after a motor vehicle accident in Minneapolis. Granulomas were noted on histopathology of the transplanted liver. Investigations: CXR: diffuse, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates Serum Aspergillus galactomannan positive with an index of 1.2 (cut-off for positivity ≥0.5) BAL fluid: fungal cultures positive after 17 days. White to brown colonies with a fine cottony texture seen The same organism was recovered from the lysis-centrifugation blood culture
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Histoplasma capsulatum The patient has disseminated histoplasmosis, a disease endemic in the midwestern United States. The presence of granulomas in the transplanted liver suggests donor-derived disease which typically occurs in the early posttransplant period as in this case. Galactomannan, a polysaccharide present in the cell wall of several fungi, is released during host infection. Serum galactomannan can be detected in invasive aspergillosis, histoplasmosis, fusariosis, and penicilliosis (but not mucormycosis). In contrast to Aspergillus, Histoplasma may be recovered from blood cultures in cases of disseminated disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q15

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. Microscopic features: 45 degree angle branching, septate hyphae, narrow hyphae (3-6 microns), relatively fast growing mould in culture ~2-3 days (contrast Mucor: acute 90 degree angle, no/few septations, broader). First line treatment: Voriconazole (Mucor: ampho B). Non-antimicrobial modalities: Surgery, reduction of immunosuppression (Mucor: diabetes control and surgery). Risk factors: Diabetes, environmental/unfiltered air exposure, AIDS, bronchiectasis, previous active TB

questions.model_answer:
a) Galactomannan is a heteropolysaccharide (mannan backbone with galactofuranose side chains) that is a major constituent of the Aspergillus cell wall and is released into blood/BAL during active hyphal growth; it is detected by a double-sandwich EIA using the EB-A2 monoclonal antibody against galactofuranose, reported as an optical density index (serum cut-off >=0.5, BAL >=1.0).

b) (1) Fusarium species. (2) Penicillium/Talaromyces marneffei. (3) Histoplasma capsulatum. (4) Paecilomyces (also Trichophyton, Alternaria, and Cryptococcus galactoxylomannan cross-reaction).

c) Highest sensitivity and specificity in profoundly neutropenic haematology patients - acute leukaemia on induction chemotherapy and allogeneic HSCT recipients - screened serially (twice weekly) while not receiving mould-active prophylaxis; in this high-prevalence, angioinvasive-disease population serum sensitivity is roughly 70-80% with specificity ~90%. Performance falls in non-neutropenic hosts (solid-organ transplant, ICU, COPD, chronic granulomatous disease) where BAL galactomannan performs better than serum, and in patients on mould-active azoles/echinocandins.

cohort_answer.text: Description: Galactomannan is a polysaccharide that is a major constituent of Aspergillus cell walls that is released during fungal growth. Other positive fungi: Fusarium spp; Penicillium spp; Histoplasma capsulatum; Trichophyton spp; Paecilomyces; Cryptococcus neoformans (rarely described). Highest sensitivity/specificity population: Post-HSCT patients and heme malignancy

questions.model_answer: a) Immunocompromised host (hematologic malignancy / cellular immune defect) with concurrent cavitary lung lesions and brain abscess points to pathogens that disseminate hematogenously from the lung to the CNS. Three organisms with empiric therapy: (1) Nocardia spp. — high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus a carbapenem (imipenem or meropenem), often with amikacin for serious/CNS disease; (2) Aspergillus spp. — voriconazole; (3) Mycobacterium tuberculosis — four-drug therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) with corticosteroids. In practice, while awaiting aspiration/culture, many experts treat an immunocompromised patient empirically with high-dose meropenem (covers Nocardia, anaerobes, gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas, and possibly Listeria) plus voriconazole plus vancomycin (until MRSA excluded). (Other acceptable organisms: Cryptococcus neoformans — liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine; or Candida spp. in neutropenia.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific Nocardia regimen (TMP-SMX + carbapenem ± amikacin) and standard RIPE + steroids for TB follow IDSA/standard guidance; the chapter names the organisms and the meropenem + voriconazole + vancomycin empiric combination.

cohort_answer.text: Nocardia: TMP/SMX + imipenem/meropenem + amikacin. Aspergillus: Voriconazole. Tuberculosis: INH/RIF/ETH/PYZ + steroids. Cryptococcus neoformans: Amphotericin B + Flucytosine (treatment phase) → Fluconazole (consolidation and suppressive phases). Actinomyces (A. meyeri, odontolyticus, israelii): Penicillin + surgery for CNS. Streptococcus anginosus: Ceftriaxone. S. aureus: Vancomycin.

questions.question: Name three distinct Aspergillus syndromes and the treatment for each.

parts.text: Name three distinct Aspergillus syndromes and treatment for each.

parts_raw.text: Name 3 distinct aspergillus syndromes and treatment for each.

questions.model_answer: (1) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) – oral corticosteroids (prednisone 0.5–2 mg/kg/day tapered over 2–3 months) with itraconazole for exacerbations/steroid-sparing. (2) Aspergilloma (pulmonary fungus ball) – observe if asymptomatic; surgical resection for significant/recurrent hemoptysis. (3) Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis – voriconazole (liposomal amphotericin B or isavuconazole as alternatives).

cohort_answer.text: Allergic manifestations: ABPA (steroids 0.5-2mg/kg/day prednisone x2-3 months +/- azole during flare or if unable to taper steroids). Fungus balls (aspergilloma) - usually pulmonary (resection +/- voriconazole). Invasive aspergillosis - invasive pulmonary, disseminated, cerebral, cutaneous, bone, etc (voriconazole or L-AMB as alternative), minimum 12 weeks. Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis: without symptoms/weight loss/fatigue/loss of pulmonary function - observe without antifungal every 3-6 months; with symptoms or radiographic progression - oral itraconazole or voriconazole minimum 6 months (posaconazole third line); surgical resection if localized disease, unresponsive to medical therapy, or persistent hemoptysis. Aspergilloma: if asymptomatic observe; if symptomatic voriconazole or echinocandin after resection. ABPA: oral or inhaled steroids, if refractory then itraconazole. Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis: polypectomy+sinus washout, topical nasal steroids, oral antifungal.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Prior or concurrent anti-mould antifungal therapy – lowers circulating antigen, decreasing sensitivity (false negatives). (2) Sample source – BAL fluid has higher sensitivity than serum. (3) Piperacillin-tazobactam/other antibiotics or, in neonates, cross-reacting Bifidobacterium antigens – cause false positives, decreasing specificity (also colonized COPD/lung-transplant patients).
b) (1) Tissue biopsy showing hyphal invasion with a positive Aspergillus culture (proven disease). (2) Bronchoscopy with BAL for culture/cytology plus chest CT (BAL PCR is more specific than galactomannan).

cohort_answer.text: Decrease sensitivity: patient with CGD/Job syndrome; concomitant use of antimould agents; source of sample from serum. Decrease specificity: PipTazo and AmoxClav (historically, less of an issue now); other fungi (Penicillium, fusarium, histo); chemo (increases false positive due to gut translocation from mucositis); COPD (colonization with aspergillus); neonates (dietary intake or cross-reacting antigens with bacteria like Bifidobacterium); IVIG (1 study found false+ galactomannans post IVIG). Confirmatory investigations: CT chest +/- other imaging depending on symptoms; BAL specimens with tissue specimen for histopathology/cytology and fungal culture; galactomannan.

d) Oral glucocorticoids are the mainstay (e.g., prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day, then tapered over several months), which Mandell notes are reserved for ABPA/asthma in CF.
e) Add an azole antifungal (itraconazole; voriconazole an alternative) as a steroid-sparing adjunct.
questions.beyond_mandell: The chapter names ABPA, A. fumigatus, oral glucocorticoids and itraconazole but does not list the diagnostic criteria; the 4 criteria are from the ISHAM/CF Foundation consensus.

questions.model_answer:
a) Aspergillus fumigatus.
b) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA).
c) (1) Predisposing condition (CF or asthma). (2) Elevated total serum IgE (>1000 IU/mL). (3) Positive A. fumigatus-specific IgE or immediate skin-test reactivity. (4) At least two of: elevated A. fumigatus-specific IgG, radiographic opacities consistent with ABPA, eosinophilia >500 cells/uL in steroid-naive patients.
d) Recommended treatment: oral glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day with taper). Adjunct: an azole antifungal (itraconazole; voriconazole an alternative).
questions.beyond_mandell: Formal ABPA diagnostic criteria and IgE thresholds are from the ISHAM/CF Foundation consensus; Mandell confirms the organism, glucocorticoids and itraconazole.

cohort_answer.text: Organism: Aspergillus fumigatus. Diagnosis: most likely allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) - chronic aspergillosis does not quite fit based on diagnostic criteria. Diagnostic criteria: Predisposing condition (asthma or CF); Increased Aspergillus IgE or Type I hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus skin test; Increased Total IgE (>1000 IU/mL); at least 2 of: increased IgG to aspergillus, radiographic pulmonary opacities consistent with ABPA, eosinophilia >500 cells/uL in steroid-naive patients. Treatment: Systemic glucocorticoids are mainstay (e.g. prednisone 0.5 mg/kg daily x14 days, then every-other-day 0.5mg/kg, taper/discontinue at 3 months; total serum IgE decreases ~25% after 1 month and 60% after 2 months; 35% decrease considered good response). Adjunct: azole antifungal (itraconazole used in studies; voriconazole could be used similarly) - IDSA recommends using both steroids and azoles together.

questions.question: A man with vasculitis on steroids has ring-enhancing lesions in the brain and lung nodules. List three possible organisms and the first-line empiric treatment regimen.

parts.text: List three possible organisms and the first-line empiric treatment regimen for an immunosuppressed patient with ring-enhancing brain lesions and lung nodules.

parts_raw.text: Guy with vasculitis on steroids who has ring enhancing lesions in brain and lung nodules. List 3 possible organisms and first line empiric treatment regimen

questions.model_answer: Three organisms: (1) Nocardia species; (2) Staphylococcus aureus; (3) Streptococcus anginosus group (also consider Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Cryptococcus, Toxoplasma, Aspergillus). Empiric regimen: cover pyogenic brain abscess (e.g., ceftriaxone + vancomycin + metronidazole) PLUS anti-Nocardia therapy given the immunosuppression and combined brain/lung picture — TMP-SMX plus imipenem or meropenem, plus amikacin (or ceftriaxone/linezolid), then de-escalate after speciation and susceptibilities.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Nocardia arm is grounded in this chapter; the broader brain-abscess differential and empiric bacterial/TB/fungal coverage rest on standard CNS-infection references (Mandell brain abscess chapter/IDSA).

cohort_answer.text: Possible organisms: Nocardia, Staph aureus, Streptococcus anginosus. Empiric treatment: Ceftriaxone, vanco, metro (empiric bacterial coverage); Septra, imipenem +/- amikacin (Nocardia); TB - RIPE + steroids if meningitis; Cryptococcus - amphoB + flucytosine, then fluconazole

questions.question_raw: Q56 2023 Part 2. Invasive aspergillosis in a BMT patient. (FUNGAL)

parts.text: Give three radiographic findings consistent with invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.
What is the preferred treatment?
With acute kidney injury and prolonged QTc, what is the best treatment option?

parts_raw.text: 3 radiographic findings consistent with IPA
Preferred treatment
AKI and prolonged QTc, what is best treatment option

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Halo sign (low-attenuation rim around a nodule; early finding). (2) Air-crescent sign (late, with neutrophil recovery). (3) Dense nodular infiltrates and/or pleural-based, wedge-shaped densities or cavitation.
b) Voriconazole (alternatives: liposomal amphotericin B or isavuconazole).
c) Isavuconazole – it shortens the QTc and requires no renal dose adjustment (avoids the QT prolongation of voriconazole and the nephrotoxicity of amphotericin B; IV voriconazole's cyclodextrin vehicle is also a concern in renal failure).

cohort_answer.text:
3 radiographic findings (Mandell IPA CT findings): diffuse nodular infiltrates; halo sign (density surrounded by a ring of low-attenuation, early sign); classic pleural-based wedge density (early, less common); cavity lesions (late); pleural effusions; 'crescent sign' (nodular lesion that cavitates).
Preferred treatment (IDSA Aspergillus Guidelines): Voriconazole. Alternates: ampho B liposomal, isavuconazole, or other lipid formulations of ampho B. Echinocandin monotherapy not recommended.
Best option with AKI/QTc prolongation: For AKI - Voriconazole (oral) or isavuconazole do not require dose adjustment; IV voriconazole contains cyclodextrin which theoretically accumulates renally, but not clinically demonstrated; IDSA states relative benefits/risks of IV voriconazole in renal failure should be individualized. For QTc prolongation: Isavuconazole, which 'shortens the QTc, clinical significance unclear'.

questions.model_answer: a) Hyphae thickness: Zygomycetes (Mucorales) - broad, wide, uneven diameter (3-25 um), ribbon-like; Aspergillus - narrow, uniform width (approx 3-5 um). Angle of branching: Zygomycetes - wide, nondichotomous, irregular branching at occasional right angles (approx 90 degrees); Aspergillus - regular dichotomous branching at acute angles (approx 45 degrees). Septate or aseptate: Zygomycetes - mostly aseptate (pauciseptate); Aspergillus - septate.
questions.beyond_mandell: Aspergillus values (narrow ~3-5 um, acute ~45 degree dichotomous branching, septate) are the standard histopathology contrast; Mandell text describes the Mucorales side directly.

Q19 (2007) Brain + Lung lesions
Man with AML getting chemo with 2 large cavitary lung lesions

parts.text: List 3 possible organisms.
Voriconazole is started and he develops sinus necrosis. What is the organism?
What is the treatment?

parts_raw.text: A) 3 possible organisms
B) Voriconazole started, develops sinus necrosis. Organism?
C) Treatment

questions.model_answer: a) Three possible causes of cavitary lung lesions in a neutropenic AML patient: (1) Aspergillus species (invasive pulmonary aspergillosis); (2) agents of mucormycosis (Mucorales); (3) Nocardia species (other reasonable answers: bacterial - Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, anaerobes/Streptococcus anginosus; or Mycobacterium tuberculosis). b) Agents of mucormycosis (most commonly Rhizopus) - breakthrough infection is characteristic when fungal sinusitis with necrosis develops on voriconazole, which lacks activity against Mucorales. c) (1) Rapid reversal of predisposing factors and, in neutropenia, consider granulocyte transfusion/G-CSF; (2) urgent surgical debridement; (3) high-dose lipid amphotericin B first-line, with step-down to posaconazole or isavuconazole once improving.
questions.beyond_mandell: The bacterial/TB/Nocardia items in the cavitary-lesion differential are established knowledge; Mandell grounds the Aspergillus and Mucorales entries and the voriconazole-breakthrough point.

cohort_answer.text:
A) Bacterial: S. anginosus, Anaerobic (oral flora), TB, Nocardia, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae. Fungal: Cryptococcus, Aspergillus, Mucormycosis.

B) Agents of mucormycosis: Rhizopus species (47%), Mucor species (18%), Cunninghamella bertholletiae (7%), Apophysomyces elegans (5%), Lichtheimia (Absidia) species (5%), Saksenaea species (5%), Rhizomucor pusillus (4%).

C) Surgery; Ampho B; Posaconazole when improving/oral stepdown.

The kid dies, and the ICU is upset he died of invasive aspergillus, and wants to know about Posaconazole prophylaxis. What is the most important factor to consider before using posaconazole prophylaxis.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Prior/concurrent anti-mould therapy – decreases sensitivity. (2) BAL versus serum sample – BAL gives higher sensitivity than serum. (3) Piperacillin-tazobactam/other antibiotics (or Bifidobacterium in neonates) – false positives, decreasing specificity.
b) Diagnostics: chest CT plus bronchoscopy/BAL for culture and cytology, with serum and/or BAL galactomannan (tissue biopsy for definitive/proven diagnosis). Treatment: voriconazole (liposomal amphotericin B if voriconazole contraindicated), with reduction of immunosuppression.
c) Whether the patient is genuinely at high risk for invasive aspergillosis – posaconazole prophylaxis is guideline-recommended specifically for AML/MDS patients with prolonged neutropenia from chemotherapy and for allogeneic HSCT recipients with GVHD (also weigh adequate drug absorption/levels and interactions, and its more serious adverse events).

cohort_answer.text: Decrease sensitivity: CGD/Job syndrome; concomitant antifungal use; serum sample source. Decrease specificity: PipTazo and AmoxClav; other fungi (Penicillium, fusarium, histo); chemo (gut translocation from mucositis); COPD (colonization). Diagnostic tests: Tissue specimen for culture/histopathology/cytology; fluid; serum/BAL galactomannan; CT scan; PJP/legionella PCR; mycoplasma culture. Treatment: Empiric PipTazo/Vanco; Amphotericin B liposomal; reduce immunosuppression if possible. Posaconazole prophylaxis consideration: underlying disease state - recommend prophylaxis with posaconazole, voriconazole, and/or micafungin during prolonged neutropenia for high-risk IA patients (hematologic disorders with poorly functioning neutrophils, acute leukemia with repeated/prolonged neutropenia, prior IA before transplant); posaconazole recommended for allogeneic HSCT recipients with GVHD at high risk for IA; systemic triazole or inhaled AmB for 3-4 months after lung transplant. 3 indications for posaconazole prophylaxis shown to reduce mortality in trials: severe GVHD; primary prophylaxis in AML undergoing chemo; primary prophylaxis in MDS undergoing chemo.

questions.question: A patient with AML has a lung-and-brain cavitary syndrome. Name three pathogens with treatment for each; describe how you would investigate (excluding blood cultures); and describe how you would treat if the patient is penicillin-allergic.

parts.text: Name three pathogens and the treatment for each.
How would you investigate (not including blood cultures)?
How would you treat if the patient is allergic to penicillin?

parts_raw.text: Name 3 pathogens and tx for each
How would you investigate (not including blood cultures)?
How would you treat if this patient is allergic to penicillin?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Nocardia spp. — TMP-SMX plus a carbapenem (imipenem/meropenem), add amikacin for disseminated/CNS disease, prolonged (>=6-12 months). (2) Aspergillus spp. — voriconazole (or isavuconazole). (3) Mucorales (or, alternatively, Rhodococcus equi / Mycobacterium tuberculosis) — liposomal amphotericin B for Mucorales (RIPE for TB). b) High-resolution CT chest and MRI brain; bronchoalveolar lavage with smears for Nocardia, acid-fast bacilli, fungi and Pneumocystis, plus bacterial/fungal/mycobacterial culture and Aspergillus galactomannan; serum galactomannan/beta-D-glucan; CT-guided lung biopsy and stereotactic brain-lesion biopsy for histology and culture. c) Penicillin-allergic: cover the same organisms without a penicillin — e.g. voriconazole/liposomal amphotericin for the mould, and for Nocardia use TMP-SMX plus a carbapenem (with amikacin); carbapenems can usually be given despite penicillin allergy, or substitute linezolid/moxifloxacin for Nocardia if a beta-lactam is truly excluded.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the investigation approach (BAL panel, brain-abscess diagnosis via a probable lung agent such as Nocardia/Aspergillus/Mucorales) is grounded in Ch. 305 (pp. 3624-3625); the specific antimicrobial regimens are from Mandell organism-specific chapters/IDSA guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Bacteria: Nocardia (TMP-SMX + Imipenem/Mero plus Amikacin if multiorgan, 6 weeks IV then PO, 2 drugs for at least a year); Rhodococcus equi (Vanco or Carbapenem + FQ/AG/macrolide/rif combination, minimum 10-14 days up to 2 months); TB (RIPE); S. aureus (Clox or Vanco); S. anginosus (Ceftriaxone); Actinomyces (penicillin G or ampicillin, IV run-in 2-6 weeks, usually >3 months). Fungi: Aspergillus (Voriconazole); Cryptococcus (Liposomal AmB + Flucytosine x2 weeks then Fluconazole); Histoplasmosis (liposomal AmB then itraconazole). Investigations: brain abscess biopsy for bacterial/fungal culture; BAL for bacterial/fungal culture and gram stain; lung biopsy; TTE. PCN allergic: Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole + TMP-SMX; to target Nocardia: Imi/Mero + Amikacin + Septra.

parts.text: What is the organism (genus)?
What is the syndrome?
What 4 diagnostic tests?
What is the preferred treatment and one possible alternate/adjunct?

parts_raw.text: What bug (genus).
b. What syndrome?
c. What 4 diagnostic tests?
d. What preferred treatment and one possible alternate/adjunct?

questions.model_answer:
a) Aspergillus.
b) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) — a long-term allergic (Th2) response to Aspergillus, with an incidence of ~7% in cystic fibrosis.
c) (1) Immediate skin-test reactivity to Aspergillus (or A. fumigatus); (2) Total serum IgE concentration (>417 IU/mL [1000 ng/mL], typically >1000 IU/mL); (3) Elevated serum IgE and/or IgG antibody to A. fumigatus; (4) Serum precipitating antibodies to A. fumigatus. (Supporting: peripheral blood eosinophilia >500 cells/uL, positive sputum culture/hyphae, central bronchiectasis on CT.)
d) Preferred: corticosteroids (oral prednisone 0.5-2 mg/kg/day, max 60 mg/day, for exacerbations, tapered over 2-3 months) — the mainstay. Alternate/adjunct: itraconazole 200 mg/day for 16 weeks, which reduces corticosteroid use, lowers IgE, and improves lung function (voriconazole or posaconazole when itraconazole fails).

cohort_answer.text: a) Aspergillus. b) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). c) Aspergillus serum IgE levels; total serum IgE concentration; elevated Aspergillus IgG; Aspergillus positive precipitin test; Aspergillus positive skin test. d) Systemic steroids + itraconazole for 16 weeks (steroids are mainstay; IDSA 2016 recommends concomitant PO itraconazole to reduce antigenic stimulation and be steroid-sparing; ATS 2009 recommends itraconazole only as steroid-sparing or if not responding to steroids alone).

parts.text: Identify the most likely pathogen on the following illustrations.

parts_raw.text: Identify the most likely pathogen on the following illustrations

questions.model_answer: (1) Blastomyces dermatitidis — 8-15 um round multinucleated broad-based budding yeast (large pore, daughter cell attached until near mother's size). (2) Aspergillus spp. — 2-5 um septate hyphae of even diameter with acute-angle (Y-shaped, dichotomous) branching; propensity for vascular invasion. (3) Pneumocystis jirovecii — 3.5-7 um nonbudding cup/cysts, black on GMS with central dot, clustered in alveoli in eosinophilic amorphous material. Contrast with agents of mucormycosis — 4-15 um-wide, rarely septate hyphae of uneven diameter branching at broad (near 90-degree) angles.

cohort_answer.text: Blastomyces (broad-based budding yeast); Aspergillus (septate with acute angle branching); Pneumocystis jiroveci. Remember - mucor (thicker aseptate, 90 degree branching).
